text:
Citigroup $C underestimated its risk-weighted assets by about $35B after incorrectly recording trades at its UK securities unit.

The bank used an internal risk model that regulators hadn't approved for those transactions. When the trades were recalculated using the correct model, the amount of assets used to determine Citi's required capital reserves jumped by roughly $35B.

Citi says it identified and fixed the issue this summer and injected additional capital into its European subsidiary to restore its financial buffers.

The bank says the subsidiary remained above regulatory minimum capital requirements throughout.

name: Cullen Roche
zh_summary: Cullen Roche explains basic bank accounting: deposits are assets for holders and liabilities for banks; reserves are bank assets and Fed liabilities to banks only, not to depositors. Individuals cannot hold reserves; only banks can. Cash withdrawal is the sole way to hold a Fed liability.
en_summary: Cullen Roche explains basic bank accounting: deposits are assets for holders and liabilities for banks; reserves are bank assets and Fed liabilities to banks only, not to depositors. Individuals cannot hold reserves; only banks can. Cash withdrawal is the sole way to hold a Fed liability.
text:
This is basic accounting. When you have a bank deposit you hold an asset and the bank has a liability. Reserves are an asset for the bank and a liability of the Fed. But the Fed's liability is to the bank, not to you. You don't have a claim on reserves because they aren't your asset and they aren't the bank's liability to you. Your claim is on the bank, full stop.

You can't even hold reserves. Only banks and a handful of other institutions with Fed accounts can. When you send money to someone at another bank, your bank settles with their bank in reserves. Your deposit goes away and they get a new one, but the reserves never touch your hands.

The one time you end up holding a Fed liability is when you withdraw cash. Your bank swaps reserves for paper currency and hands it to you. That's a Fed liability, but it's a different one. It isn't reserves.

text:
Anthropic starts trading tomorrow. $81.3 billion at $83 a share. The largest IPO in history, ahead of SpaceX's $75B in June.

The market has already paid for it. SPY is −5.55% over the last 20 trading days. QQQ is −9.06%.

The question now: does the drain keep going once $81 billion is in one stock, or was the selling the drain?

We tested it. 54 of the largest US-listed IPOs since 2007. SPY and QQQ forward returns from each listing-day close.

In the 20 trading days after listing, mega-IPOs haven't drained liquidity. The market has done better than usual.

-SPY 20-day forward: +1.90%, 83% win rate (p < 0.0001)
-QQQ 20-day forward: +2.44%, 80% win rate (p = 0.0001)

SPY on any random day: +0.78% over 20 days. After a mega-IPO it beats its own baseline by +1.12% (p = 0.004).

The $15B+ tier: Visa +5.16%, GM +3.62%, Meta +3.59%, Alibaba -6.09%. Three of four positive.

Now the live tests. 2026 gave us two IPOs bigger than anything in the study:

1. SpaceX ($75B, June 12): SPY +1.36%, QQQ -0.23% over 20 days.
2. SK hynix ($26.5B, July 10): SPY +2.43%, QQQ -0.34%.

SPY rose both times, short of the +1.90% average. QQQ was flat both times. No drain. But no tech-led rally either.

Our study starts at the listing, so it can't tell us whether the selling was caused by the IPO. The closest precedent is Meta in 2012: SPY fell −4.98% in the 20 days before, then rose +3.59% in the 20 after. 

The caveat: Anthropic is 3.7x Alibaba, the largest IPO in our historical sample. Two live tests
